items.title: How Much You Need to Exercise for Better Sleep, According to Experts
items.author: Dean Stattmann
items.summary: Ever notice how some workouts put you to sleep while others make you feel like someone switched out your vitamins for caffeine pills? You’re not going crazy.
items.text:
Ever notice how some workouts put you to sleep while others make you feel like someone switched out your vitamins for caffeine pills? You’re not going crazy. Exercise can significantly impact your sleep—for better or for worse—depending on how, and when, you work out.

Unfortunately, the exercise-sleep relationship is not as straightforward as the internet’s sleepmaxxers might lead you to believe. While research has unlocked some valuable insights that you can start putting into practice later tonight, there’s still a lot we don’t know. "Part of what's vexing about this is we don't have the mechanism totally locked down,” says James Wyatt, PhD, clinical sleep disorder specialist at Rush University System for Health in Chicago.

"It's also important to caveat that, while the data is enormously helpful, there's so much intra-individual variability,” says Kristen Holmes, PhD, global head of human performance and principal scientist at Whoop. At the end of the day (literally), sleep is a complex chemical equation that differs to various degrees from person to person.

But back to those valuable insights. From morning HIIT workouts that reset your circadian rhythm to an evening workout to hack your body’s natural cooling system, here are some of the best ways to use exercise to fall asleep faster, according to experts.

Working out in general won’t make you fall asleep faster

Exercise can certainly reduce the time it takes to fall asleep, but not for the reason that many wellness influencers would have you think—that is, by spurring your body’s natural production of adenosine, a sleep-inducing compound that is also a byproduct of exercise.

Your body’s cells rely on a molecule called adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, for energy. It’s a universal fuel source that powers everything from muscle contractions to brain function to simply existing. As ATP is utilized, it produces a compound called adenosine. Adenosine is not a waste product. In fact, it is highly valuable. “In muscle, adenosine helps to reduce inflammation and limit damage during periods of metabolic stress,” says Dr. Holmes. Meanwhile, in the brain, adenosine accumulates throughout the day, gradually making you feel sleepier. “In sleep science, this is called ‘sleep pressure,’” says Dr. Holmes.

So it seems perfectly plausible that the key to falling asleep faster would simply be to exercise. More exertion equals more adenosine and therefore greater sleep pressure. A 2007 study published in the journal Neuroscience actually found that when rats engaged in intense exercise, the levels of adenosine in their brains increased significantly.

But that’s not how it works in humans. "Adenosine can do an awful lot of different things in the brain and in the body, but we have to separate these,” says Dr. Wyatt. This is because adenosine doesn’t cross the blood-brain barrier—the wrapping around your brain that selectively allows certain chemicals in and not others. “If you build up adenosine in your body as a byproduct of exercising, that will not influence what happens in your brain,” Dr. Wyatt says. “That adenosine doesn't make it into the brain.”

Make no mistake, adenosine is still crucial for sleep in humans. "Adenosine on its own is one of the major chemicals that helps us fall asleep at night and get deep sleep for the first couple of hours,” Dr. Wyatt says. But only adenosine that is created in the brain will ultimately contribute to increasing sleep pressure.

The timing of your workout may be more important than the intensity

In terms of how hard or you need to work out in order to fall asleep faster, experts aren’t entirely sure of this, or if it even matters all that much. "We don't have a lot of great data on the intensity of exercise that's needed,” says Dr. Wyatt. The main reason for this, it seems, is that exercise’s ability to improve sleep is likely not a direct function of intensity—or any single factor, for that matter—but rather a combination of variables, including timing. For example, working out at a high intensity could be helpful in the morning, but detrimental later on in the day.

"One way that exercise could indirectly influence sleep is that it strengthens your circadian rhythm—that 24-hour daily rhythm of alertness during the day and sleepiness at night,” says Dr. Wyatt. In other words, working out earlier in the day can help your body understand that it’s daytime, and that in a couple of hours it will be time to sleep. But slow cardio isn’t going to cut it. “In animals, if you look at a rat or a mouse, the time during the day when you give them access to exercise dramatically shifts their circadian rhythm,” Dr. Wyatt says. “But in humans, exercise is a very weak signal for aligning ourselves to the 24-hour day, so it has to be an awful lot of exercise to have a notable effect.” (We recommend giving this HIIT workout a try.)

As for going all out in the evening, in a 2025 study published in the journal Nature Communications, researchers observed that high-strain workouts done within four hours of bedtime had a range of detrimental effects on sleep. In the study, data from nearly 15,000 Whoop members across more than four million nights revealed that an intense evening workout can delay sleep onset, reduce total sleep duration, and degrade overall sleep quality. “Basically, what we found is that intense exercise ending within four hours of going to bed was associated with these changes in sleep,” says Dr. Holmes. “When you're exercising at a high intensity, you're releasing adrenaline, cortisol, and epinephrine, so it's going to take time afterwards for that to dissipate.”

How to work out to fall asleep faster

According to Dr. Wyatt and Dr. Holmes, there are basically two types of workouts that may potentially help you fall asleep faster. The first one, as mentioned, is a high-intensity session during the day—the earlier the better—to help click your circadian rhythm into sync with the day. Ideally, you’ll want to also include some natural sunlight in the equation or, better yet, train outdoors. “From a circadian perspective, you want to create as much contrast between the day and the night as possible,” says Dr. Holmes.

The other option is an evening workout—albeit a relatively light one. According to the Whoop study data, when people engaged in a low-intensity evening workout, they experienced better sleep quality than those who didn’t exercise at all—and they only needed one hour of buffer time between training and going to bed.

The sleep-inducing power of a low-intensity evening workout has nothing to do with your circadian rhythm and everything to do with body temperature. As you approach bedtime, your body is naturally configured to move heat away from its core—a process that contributes to feelings of sleepiness. Exercise, of course, does the opposite and raises your core temperature, but it also makes your body work harder to lower it. According to John Hopkins Medicine, core temperature starts to fall about 30–90 minutes after exercising. Timing your workout to end 1–2 hours before bedtime—which, according to Dr. Wyatt, also happens to be right around the time your brain starts releasing melatonin—effectively layers that post-workout temperature drop on top of your body’s natural cooling process, creating the perfect sleep storm. “Exercise ramps up body temperature even more, and therefore it has an even steeper drop,” Dr. Wyatt says. “The steepness of that drop in body temperature is what might be associated with the ability to fall asleep faster.”

“The general guidance is: Evening exercise can help sleep, too close to bed is bad, and too far away from bedtime may be ineffective. But again, there are those individual differences,” Dr. Wyatt says. “This is why it's challenging. It's not going to be just a single recipe that says, ‘Okay, do this one thing and sleep suddenly gets better.’ You have to find the combination that works for you.”

"We don't have a lot of great data on the intensity of exercise that's needed,” says Dr. Wyatt. The main reason for this, it seems, is that exercise’s ability to improve sleep is likely not a direct function of intensity—or any single factor, for that matter—but rather a combination of variables, including timing. For example, working out at a high intensity could be helpful in the morning, but detrimental later on in the day.

"One way that exercise could indirectly influence sleep is that it strengthens your circadian rhythm—that 24-hour daily rhythm of alertness during the day and sleepiness at night,” says Dr. Wyatt. In other words, working out earlier in the day can help your body understand that it’s daytime, and that in a couple of hours it will be time to sleep. But slow cardio isn’t going to cut it. “In animals, if you look at a rat or a mouse, the time during the day when you give them access to exercise dramatically shifts their circadian rhythm,” Dr. Wyatt says. “But in humans, exercise is a very weak signal for aligning ourselves to the 24-hour day, so it has to be an awful lot of exercise to have a notable effect.” (We recommend giving this HIIT workout a try.)

As for going all out in the evening, in a 2025 study published in the journal Nature Communications, researchers observed that high-strain workouts done within four hours of bedtime had a range of detrimental effects on sleep. In the study, data from nearly 15,000 Whoop members across more than four million nights revealed that an intense evening workout can delay sleep onset, reduce total sleep duration, and degrade overall sleep quality. “Basically, what we found is that intense exercise ending within four hours of going to bed was associated with these changes in sleep,” says Dr. Holmes. “When you're exercising at a high intensity, you're releasing adrenaline, cortisol, and epinephrine, so it's going to take time afterwards for that to dissipate.”
How to work out to fall asleep faster

According to Dr. Wyatt and Dr. Holmes, there are basically two types of workouts that may potentially help you fall asleep faster. The first one, as mentioned, is a high-intensity session during the day—the earlier the better—to help click your circadian rhythm into sync with the day. Ideally, you’ll want to also include some natural sunlight in the equation or, better yet, train outdoors. “From a circadian perspective, you want to create as much contrast between the day and the night as possible,” says Dr. Holmes.

The other option is an evening workout—albeit a relatively light one. According to the Whoop study data, when people engaged in a low-intensity evening workout, they experienced better sleep quality than those who didn’t exercise at all—and they only needed one hour of buffer time between training and going to bed.

The sleep-inducing power of a low-intensity evening workout has nothing to do with your circadian rhythm and everything to do with body temperature. As you approach bedtime, your body is naturally configured to move heat away from its core—a process that contributes to feelings of sleepiness. Exercise, of course, does the opposite and raises your core temperature, but it also makes your body work harder to lower it. According to John Hopkins Medicine, core temperature starts to fall about 30–90 minutes after exercising. Timing your workout to end 1–2 hours before bedtime—which, according to Dr. Wyatt, also happens to be right around the time your brain starts releasing melatonin—effectively layers that post-workout temperature drop on top of your body’s natural cooling process, creating the perfect sleep storm. “Exercise ramps up body temperature even more, and therefore it has an even steeper drop,” Dr. Wyatt says. “The steepness of that drop in body temperature is what might be associated with the ability to fall asleep faster.”

“The general guidance is: Evening exercise can help sleep, too close to bed is bad, and too far away from bedtime may be ineffective. But again, there are those individual differences,” Dr. Wyatt says. “This is why it's challenging. It's not going to be just a single recipe that says, ‘Okay, do this one thing and sleep suddenly gets better.’ You have to find the combination that works for you.”

items.title: Fukushima’s Old Farming Rituals Come to Life in Haga Hideo’s Photography
items.summary: During the 1950s the photographer Haga Hideo captured traditional folk festivals in Fukushima Prefecture. Now the memories in his work have come back home,
items.text:
During the 1950s the photographer Haga Hideo captured traditional folk festivals in Fukushima Prefecture. Now the memories in his work have come back home, with the presentation of his photographic data to locals who are already putting it to work to bring these traditions back to life.

Worshipping Tanokami: The Deity of Abundant Harvests

Before becoming a professional photographer, the pioneering folklore photographer Haga Hideo (1921–2022) worked as a translator at a news agency. That career came to an end in 1952 when the agency disbanded. For a change of scene, he headed to Fukushima Prefecture, where his father was from. While staying with relatives in what is now the city of Iwaki, he encountered a New Year ritual performed among farming families.

Prior to Japan’s rapid economic development in the years after World War II, folk beliefs in the tanokami rice deity were alive and well in many parts of the country. In Fukushima, the family patriarch and his eldest son would gather the straw from the rice harvested the previous fall to create a yorishiro, an object to beckon a deity, to welcome Shōgatsu-sama, the spirit thought to bring bountiful crops. In spring, this spirit would reappear in the rice paddies to make the rice ripen; it would then leave after the fall harvest, returning to the mountains where it dwelled.

The idea of an invisible deity responsible for the bounty of nature inspired Haga, who turned his camera lens to deity-welcoming ceremonies and their carefully crafted ritual implements and offerings. Casting a closer eye on this unadorned spiritual culture, he was reminded of marebito, the concept of a divine spirit visiting from the “other world” that he had learned about from the folklorist and ethnologist Orikuchi Shinobu (1887–1953) during his university studies.

The altar for worshipping Shōgatsu-sama on the first day of the new year. (© Haga Hideo)

A ceremony to pray for a good harvest, performed after a paddy dried out during winter has been worked with a hoe in preparation for planting. (© Haga Hideo)

Preparing mochibana, bits of mochi pounded rice threaded onto branches, as a stand-in for Shōgatsu-sama, on January 13. (© Haga Hideo)

A divination ritual conducted on the evening of January 14. Twelve soybeans are roasted in the irori sunken hearth and used to predict the weather for the coming year according to the degree of charring. (© Haga Hideo)

Torigoya is conducted even today on koshōgatsu, January 15. Bamboo, straw, and New Year decorations are burned to return Shōgatsu-sama to the heavens. (© Haga Hideo)

Warmed by hearty oden stew, children gather in a hut to sing a song to drive away birds, which eat the grain the fields, in the hope of an abundant harvest. (© Haga Hideo)

Passing On the Traditions of Iwaki

In the foreword to Tanokami: Nihon no inasaku girei (Deity of the Rice Paddies: The Rice Cultivation Rituals of Japan), Haga’s first collection of photos taken in Iwaki, he explained why he had chosen to pursue this work there.

For 2,000 years, the Japanese people have grown rice, around which the belief in tanokami and associated rituals has developed. Many Japanese customs and myths have been influenced by tanokami, providing insight into how rice cultivation rituals are reflected in daily life and social structures . . . Today, modern science has made good harvests possible without the intervention of tanokami. Progress in agricultural technology and the modernization of farm life are rapidly eroding traditional village society, in which religious beliefs, crop production, and entertainment were intertwined. This is a last opportunity to record the rituals associated with rice production for posterity.

As Haga had foreseen, the rituals around rice growing were rapidly becoming simplified or had disappeared altogether. Meanwhile, the significance of rites centering around tanokami, such as Hiroshima Prefecture’s Mibu no Hana Taue and Ishikawa Prefecture’s Oku-Noto Aenokoto, has been recognized with their collective inscription by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Haga, who made recording folklore for posterity his lifework, passed away in 2022 at the age of 101.

Iwaki, where Haga got his start as a folklore photographer, is today on the verge of losing its traditional farming culture. The Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing, which opened in 1999, is leading efforts to preserve what is left of those traditions. The museum collects and displays all manner of artifacts related to local life.

Five traditional thatched-roof houses, dismantled and transported from various parts of Iwaki, have been re-erected in the museum’s vast grounds. Meticulously preserved, they reproduce a premodern farm village. On display inside the houses are farming tools of the era; visitors can also try their hand at working in the fields and paddies outside. Iwaki schoolchildren visit here as part of their social studies lessons, and on weekends, adults can participate in workshops to learn about the local culture.

The permanent exhibit showcases farm life from the Edo period (1603–1868) to the present. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Farm tools and artifacts, including a life-sized figure (at left) created to protect the village from evil, have been collected from various parts of Iwaki. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

A traditional home from the latter half of the nineteenth century stands in the park. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

The interior is mostly untouched. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Mochibana prepared by children are displayed. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Top: The Jangara Nenbutsu Odori folk entertainment performed during the midsummer bon period. Bottom: A child is taught how to make a New Year decoration. (Courtesy Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing)

In the summer of 2026, Haga’s son Haga Hinata visited the folklore museum to donate 46 film rolls’ worth of digitalized photo data, to help teach local history. Sorting through the collection, the museum selected photos of folklore entertainment that had died out more than 30 years before, including them in a special exhibit during the summer.

According to curator Ōta Yūhi, “Photos depicting farming in Iwaki in the postwar years are very rare, and they are invaluable for scholarly research. For example, the folklorist Seki Keigo [1899–1990] remarked that he had understood narikizeme, the act of hitting a fruit tree with a knife to cast a spell to ensure a bountiful crop, from a written description, but that Haga’s photo was the first time he had actually seen the action performed.”

A special exhibit planned for the fall on the theme of “straw” features donated photos illustrating Shōgatsu-sama, torigoya, and other traditions. The photos will also be used for school lectures by outside speakers and are included in the Iwaki Digital Museum showcasing cultural resources. Haga says “I’m very happy that the folklore museum values local folklore and that I was able to entrust it with my father’s photos.”

Top: Haga Hinata, at right, presents digitalized photo data to museum director Yajima Noriyuki. Below: The Folk Entertainment of Iwaki exhibition, which runs until September 27, includes photos taken in 1960. (© Uzawa Akihiko)

Although acreage under cultivation has decreased, rice-growing continues. The photo at top (© Haga Hideo) shows the hamlet of Kamikamado, where Haga photographed New Year ceremonies in 1953; below (© Uzawa Akihiko) is the same setting today.

Rich Folklore Traditions Live On

Haga also called on the Fukushima Museum in Aizu-Wakamatsu to donate the digitalized contents of 138 rolls of film containing photos taken throughout the prefecture. His father’s photos had been included in an exhibition that traveled to Beijing and Rome in 2012, the year after the Great East Japan Earthquake. Haga’s presentation took place on the occasion of the return of the exhibition to the Fukushima Museum.

At the ceremony, Ōsato Masaki, the museum’s curator in charge of folklore, displayed the actual ritual implements and crafts that the photos had recorded. He explained: “Along with actual physical examples, photos are vital for explaining traditional rituals. Haga Hideo’s photos, especially those in which he focused on capturing the essence of those rituals, are priceless.”

In addition, several film strips were digitalized in chronological order, giving a good idea of the sequence of events taking place. The 1960 photos showing festivities in the town of Miharu are particularly interesting.

One sequence shows the moment a bride enters the groom’s home, a once-in-a-lifetime occasion. According to Ōsato, “Haga must have negotiated beforehand with the family, since he took photos from inside the home.” He expressed surprise that the sequence of photos “shows the go-between and a female neighbor removing the bride’s umbrellalike wicker headgear and guests chanting the celebratory ‘Takasago’ song from the nō play of the same name. These are the kinds of photos depicting a ceremony that one might expect to see in school textbooks on folklore.”

A photo from the wedding. Haga recorded the entire proceedings, from the exchange of yuinō betrothal gifts to reporting the marriage to the local shrine’s tutelary deity. (© Haga Hideo)

Top: A Fukushima Museum display of folk implements similar to those depicted in the donated photo collection. Bottom: Museum director Matsuyama Masayuki, at left, expresses pleasure at receiving the collection, which he considers a valuable resource for communicating Fukushima’s past way of life. (© Nippon.com)

Presenting the collection, Haga said, “Fukushima’s festivals are an important element in human relations. They haven’t really been in the public eye since the March 2011 earthquake, but I hope that these photos will make local people proud of their folk culture.”

A similar collection of digitalized photos, taken in the 1950s, was gifted to Kagoshima Prefecture’s Amami Ōshima in the summer of 2025; activities relating to the collection have been ongoing there. The Amami Museum held an exhibit commemorating the donation of the photos this summer and is also planning a traveling exhibition to other parts of Japan, starting with Kobe, targeting former residents of Okinoerabujima, one of the Amami islands. Perhaps a similar activity can be organized in Fukushima to communicate the local culture to younger generations.

The Kohata no Hata Matsuri in Nihonmatsu, where a coming-of-age rite for 15-year-olds includes transiting through a narrow passage to symbolically “emerge” into adulthood, is still conducted today. (© Haga Hideo)

A traditional rite in the town of Asakawa, held to protect fields and paddies from strong winds, celebrates a deity known as Kazebukuro-sama. (© Haga Hideo)

Artisans making traditional handcraft Aizu erōsoku candles. (© Haga Hideo)

(Originally published in Japanese. Reporting and text by Fujiwara Tomoyuki of Nippon.com. Banner image: A man carrying the straw bundles used in the Shōgatsu-sama New Year ritual, at left, and a man striking a fruit tree in the narikizeme rite. © Haga Hideo.)

items.title: 'Today the game was unprotected' - Arteta fumes but Arsenal survive
items.summary:
Arsenal's duality was there for all to see in their 2-0 win at Sunderland: gritty defence and moments of genius.

But things could have turned out very
items.text:
Arsenal's duality was there for all to see in their 2-0 win at Sunderland: gritty defence and moments of genius.

But things could have turned out very differently had a crucial 121-second period gone the other way.

After close to an hour of physical, full-blooded football, Sunderland were given a penalty when Ezri Konsa fouled Dan Ballard at a corner.

It proved the turning point - David Raya tipped Enzo le Fee's spot kick on to the post, and just over two minutes later, Arsenal substitute Bruno Guimaraes crashed in the opener off the underside of the crossbar.

Arteta's side left the north-east of England with their ninth successive Premier League victory. Not since the days of the Invincibles, in 2003-04, have the Gunners done that.

Yet Arteta was furious about the Sunderland penalty that could have cost his side.

"It's a judo roll from the opponent. Ezri [Konsa] does nothing. Just watch it," Arteta told BBC Match of the Day.

"We have a lot of cameras and VAR, we have to take responsibility to protect the game. Today the game was unprotected and it could have cost us the game and the momentum which is a really, really serious thing."

Referee John Brooks took a few seconds to point to the penalty spot after Ballard and Konsa hit the ground, but once he did the VAR stuck with his decision.

Konsa was certainly committing a foul, though Ballard did appear to have a hold of the Arsenal man.

"This should never happen, it's not fair, and I am sad, very sad, in that sense," said Arteta, who was booked in the first half for repeatedly leaving his technical area.

"I'm making it very clear publicly because it's for the game, it's not only for Arsenal, this cannot happen at this level.

"It's not acceptable, I've watched it 20 times and can't think of why it was given."

This season, Premier League referees have been instructed to clamp down on grappling at corners, something that became a big talking point last term.

"With the new laws trying to get rid of the grappling, Konsa is all over Ballard. You have to be looking at the ball," former England midfielder Karen Carney said on TNT Sports.

"Ballard was holding Konsa's arm but you run the risk," added former Arsenal defender Martin Keown.

"They want to stamp down on it so there is no point arguing about it."

However, Arteta was not alone in questioning the decision.

"It's absolutely not a penalty. He has got it completely wrong, Konsa's shoulder is pulled down by Ballard and he lands on top," former Wales defender Ashley Williams said on BBC Match of the Day.

"It's like a perfect toss in judo. It's very clever by Ballard but in no way is it a penalty."

Though Arteta spoke more about the awarding of the penalty rather than Raya's saving of it, there is no denying that the Spanish goalkeeper's intervention changed the direction of the match.

The save - only Raya's second penalty stop in the Premier League - came at a time when Sunderland were putting the defending champions under pressure.

Though Le Fee telegraphed his effort, Raya had to be at full stretch to tip it on to the post. Until that point, the goalkeeper had largely been a spectator.

"He keeps us alive in the game, that unbelievable moment saving the penalty," Guimaraes told TNT Sports.

"I think after this moment we [took from it] a big confidence to play forward and score our goal."

"This penalty save is exceptional. He gets out so quick," former Brentford manager Thomas Frank - the man who signed Raya - said on BBC Match of the Day.

"For me he's the best goalkeeper in the Premier League and one of the best in the world."

After building last season's title-winning campaign on a stubborn defence, the Gunners have begun this season with five clean sheets in six matches in all competitions, including in all three away matches.

"It is a fantastic win and the ground work was done by the defence. They have weathered the storm and the goalkeeper steps up and makes a wonderful save," Keown said.

"He is very important to Arsenal and what they achieve. He was magnificent and doesn't get the credit he deserves."

Though seething about the penalty, Arteta took the opportunity during his post-match media conference to praise his side's defensive efforts.

"We knew we would have to go through some difficult and chaotic moments to have the right to win this game," he said. "But we have done it."

On a night when Arsenal were not at their fluid best, one hero was not going to be enough.

Guimaraes stepped up with a goal of the season contender, a curling effort from the edge of the penalty area.

The Brazilian midfielder has had a tough start to life at Arsenal since his £75m summer move from Newcastle, failing to start a match since the Community Shield.

Now recovered from a minor hamstring injury, he showed exactly what he can offer.

"That goal is about personality and character. It was him saying: I am going to make my mark at this football club," Keown said.

"He has been watching on the sidelines, but has said: 'Take a look at me - this is what I can do.'

"Boy did he shut the crowd up. A class player, going to the next level."

Of all the teams to announce himself against, Guimaraes chose the arch-rivals of his former employers Newcastle.

"It was a beautiful goal. Everyone knows my past, I had an amazing history at Newcastle," Guimaraes told TNT Sports.

"But now I'm trying to create a new history here and I start with the right foot."

This match could have turned out very differently for Arsenal, but in the end, it was heroes old and new that got the job done.

items.title: Toothless Spurs blank again as new era turns into a false dawn
items.summary:
The banner held aloft by a Tottenham Hotspur supporter before kick-off was not so much a plea for action as a cry for help.

"Please Score A Goal" was the
items.text:
The banner held aloft by a Tottenham Hotspur supporter before kick-off was not so much a plea for action as a cry for help.

"Please Score A Goal" was the message brandished in the direction of the Spurs players as they came out against Everton in search of their first in the Premier League this season.

After another goalless 45 minutes, there was a compelling case for a hasty rewrite asking "Please Have A Shot" as, for all their possession, Roberto de Zerbi's expensively assembled side struggled to get anywhere near Jordan Pickford's goal.

And so it went on in an increasingly angry and frustrated atmosphere inside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium as Spurs' goalless league streak extended to 407 minutes as a stuttering start to what was meant to be brave new era continued.

It was the first time they have failed to score in their opening four league games across all four tiers - and also in four successive Premier League matches since September 2006.

The grim statistic would be bad enough in any circumstances, but it is even worse after Spurs spent in excess of £300m in the summer, much of it designed to give De Zerbi's side an added edge.

Instead, they are a blunt instrument.

This was the first Premier League goalless draw, in the 140th game, at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

On this evidence, there will be more.

It may seem early days for an apology to the supporters, but De Zerbi felt the need as he said: "I'm sorry to the fans. We are sorry to the fans.

"They were fantastic, especially in the first part of the game because when they see the team is playing well, pushing to find the solution, they were inside the pitch with my players. Then the reaction of the fans is normal. We have to say thanks all the time to them."

Everton could have actually made matters worse, but they are also short of attacking threat themselves - luckily for Spurs.

As the second half wore on, the resilient visitors actually missed the game's two best chances through Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Brennan Johnson, while the mood became increasingly sour as nerves and anxiety grew.

When £85m summer signing Mateus Fernandes had Spurs' first shot on target, the stadium rattled to the sound of ironic applause.

There was no irony when they played the ball around at the back with only seven minutes left, and when the final whistle sounded it was just like old times - or at least like last season - as jeers sent De Zerbi's players on their way.

He went through the card in an attempt to change this embarrassing barren sequence in front of goal, playing his new signings from Manchester City, Omar Marmoush and Savio, in attacking positions, with striker Dominic Solanke handed his first league start of the campaign.

As time went on and tension mounted, Mohammed Kudus and James Maddison were sent on, but it was another substitute, Lucas Bergvall, who almost snatched victory with a late long-range effort, saved by Everton goalkeeper Pickford after he had gifted the Swede possession and an opportunity.

Watching it all from close quarters was a grim-faced Richarlison, the 29-year-old Brazil striker in dispute with the club over the remaining nine months of his contract.

He was left out of De Zerbi's Premier League squad after a proposed deadline-day return to former club Everton collapsed. A switch back to Brazil with Vasco da Gama has also failed to materialise.

The 'xG' - expected goals - statistic suggests Spurs should have scored three or four goals this season, but their non-penalty xG per shot this season is just 0.066. It gives them an expected conversion rate of 6.6%.

In layman's terms, it means they are not very good when it comes to creating an attacking threat.

De Zerbi, never someone to disguise his emotions, grew more animated and irritated as the game went on, marching on to the pitch at the final whistle for an exchange with substitute Mathys Tel, though the Italian insisted he was trying to help the French winger.

"Yes, I coached him [Tel] on the pitch," De Zerbi said.

"The body shape. He is a striker and the striker can play with the shoulder on the goal.

"If we are playing with Maddison, Kudus and Savio, [Tel] has to play as a striker and the striker has to look at the goal or the cross from [Andy] Robertson.

"But I love Mathys as a player, as a guy and there is not a problem."

When any side embarks on the sort of root and branch revolution the Italian presided over this summer, it is inevitable there will be teething problems and time required for understandings and relationships to form.

And the change is understandable after two successive 17th-placed finishes in the Premier League. Indeed, Spurs' last league goal actually came against Everton on the final day of last season, courtesy of Joao Palhinha.

It kept them in the top flight, allowing them to make a fresh start for this campaign.

De Zerbi, who still has much work to do to rid Spurs of the aftershock of two poor seasons, said: "I think in the first 30 minutes we were very good but we didn't find a goal. I think in that moment we suffer too much with confidence and this is another important part for us at the moment.

"In the second half, I observed many players had a little less confidence and I don't like this. They have to be happy and understand we are in the right way.

"The players are human and they have emotions and they think with their head. My position is to help them and stay focused on the improvement we have to do. If we play 90 minutes like we did in the first 30 minutes, I think we are going to win many games."

Spurs, however, have a toothlessness that must be a concern. It is certainly a worry for the supporters who watched their players either take too long over chances or, on many occasions, pass on the responsibility.

They also ran into a rugged Everton defence, with Jarrad Branthwaite magnificent as he stepped up his claims for a place in Thomas Tuchel's next England squad after injury troubles.

For Spurs, however, there were few positives as the wait for a first Premier League win - and goal - this season goes on.

items.title: Hull stun Chelsea with Mohamed Belloumi double before João Pedro rescues a point
items.author: Jacob Steinberg at Stamford Bridge
items.summary: The chants from the away end about winning the league were sung in jest, but Hull continue to show they are here to stay. Sergej Jakirovic’s dogged,
items.text:
The chants from the away end about winning the league were sung in jest, but Hull continue to show they are here to stay. Sergej Jakirovic’s dogged, intelligent side are third in the Premier League after extending their unbeaten start to four games and can even count themselves unfortunate not to have beaten another of the Big Six after pushing Chelsea to the limit in an absorbing battle at a frustrated Stamford Bridge.

Hull were 2-1 up at half-time and they had the chances to snatch the points during the second half. It took two big saves from Emiliano Martínez to prevent an upset, but this was not a good day for the Chelsea goalkeeper or his new teammates. He was one of several at fault when Hull, having dusted themselves down after conceding from Morgan Rogers early on, went ahead through Mohamed Belloumi’s quickfire double. The ease with which Chelsea’s advantage was handed over left the normally calm and considered Xabi Alonso accusing his side of being “soft” without the ball.

Alonso craves the comfort of a forgettable win. Chelsea have been exhilarating in attack, but they cannot defend. They are conceding two goals per game and the basketball nature of Alonso’s approach has created chaos rather than control. “It’s all entertaining, but I hope that one day you say it was a boring game and we win,” he said. “It will take time. When we get the lead you still need to be competing and not to give the chance so easily for them to come back.

“Especially in the first goal, we can do much better. It was too soft to give them hope because until then we were controlling, we were creating chances, but that changed the mood. We will get better, but it’s having an impact on our performances.”

It is ridiculous that Rogers, Cole Palmer and João Pedro are having to do so much in attack. Chelsea led after seven minutes, surging forward when they left four players forward at a Hull corner. João Pedro’s pass reached Rogers and the £117m signing from Aston Villa drove past Regan Slater before beating Konstantinos Tzolaki at his near post with a low, hard and early shot from the left.

Chelsea should have pushed on after becoming the first side to breach Hull since their promotion. Pedro Neto tested Tzolakis from the right, but the hosts became vague and complacent. This was the first time they have dominated possession in a league game this season and the result was not convincing. Hull limited them to an xG of 0.89, highlighting Chelsea’s issues against low blocks, and were clinical when they attacked.

The soft defending Alonso referenced for the equaliser started with Malo Gusto failing to deal with a long punt from Tzolakis in the 28th minute. Ryan Giles outmuscled the right-back and hooked a cross to the far post. Jorrel Hato misread the Hull left-back’s delivery, leaving Belloumi to rap a shot past Martínez.

Chelsea are without a win against promoted sides in five home games. They do not smell danger, while Alonso’s decision to leave Maxence Lacroix out at centre-back and shift from a back three to a 4-2-3-1 system backfired. Hull had so much space on the flanks. They pushed again and Belloumi’s flick found Lewie Coyle, who ran off Rogers but saw his shot cleared off the line by Levi Colwill.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

skip past newsletter promotion

“The dynamic in terms of conceding, I don’t like it,” Alonso said. “Open play, set-pieces, long balls, this toughness, this competitive sense, we can do better.”

There was no response from Chelsea after Colwill turned Coyle’s shot wide. A corner came in from the left, Martínez flapped and Semi Ajayi’s header hit the bar. The ball came to Belloumi, whose shot flew in thanks to a deflection.

Alonso reacted at half-time, Hato making way for Pep Chavarría at left-back. Reece James drew a save from Tzolakis with a free-kick but Hull carried a threat on the break. They almost extended their lead when Martínez spilled a shot from Slater.

Martínez redeemed himself, blocking the rebound from McBurnie, and Chelsea soon levelled. Palmer, otherwise quiet, surprised Hull with a direct run. The No 10 drove down the left and picked out João Pedro, who lashed a shot into the roof of the net.

Hull refused to lie down. Ajayi, Giles and John Egan were outstanding at the back and the visitors maintained their shape when losing Nobel Mendy after a nasty collision with João Pedro.

Jakirovic made bold substitutions. Alonso threw Danny Welbeck on. Palmer scooped over from 20 yards and Tzolakis thwarted Rogers, but Hull had the best chance. Giles crossed again and Mohamed-Ali Cho shot straight at Martínez from close range.

Hull settled for a point. Jakirovic quashed talk of qualifying for Europe, insisting that survival remains the aim. The Bosnian has everyone pulling in the same direction. Before the start of the season he told his staff he would give them seven days off if Hull took eight points from their first five games. Mission completed with a game to spare.

Ryan Giles outmuscled the right-back and hooked a cross to the far post. Jorrel Hato misread the Hull left-back’s delivery, leaving Belloumi to rap a shot past Martínez.

Chelsea are without a win against promoted sides in five home games. They do not smell danger, while Alonso’s decision to leave Maxence Lacroix out at centre-back and shift from a back three to a 4-2-3-1 system backfired. Hull had so much space on the flanks. They pushed again and Belloumi’s flick found Lewie Coyle, who ran off Rogers but saw his shot cleared off the line by Levi Colwill.

“The dynamic in terms of conceding, I don’t like it,” Alonso said. “Open play, set-pieces, long balls, this toughness, this competitive sense, we can do better.”

There was no response from Chelsea after Colwill turned Coyle’s shot wide. A corner came in from the left, Martínez flapped and Semi Ajayi’s header hit the bar. The ball came to Belloumi, whose shot flew in thanks to a deflection.

Alonso reacted at half-time, Hato making way for Pep Chavarría at left-back. Reece James drew a save from Tzolakis with a free-kick but Hull carried a threat on the break. They almost extended their lead when Martínez spilled a shot from Slater.

Martínez redeemed himself, blocking the rebound from McBurnie, and Chelsea soon levelled. Palmer, otherwise quiet, surprised Hull with a direct run. The No 10 drove down the left and picked out João Pedro, who lashed a shot into the roof of the net.
Hull refused to lie down. Ajayi, Giles and John Egan were outstanding at the back and the visitors maintained their shape when losing Nobel Mendy after a nasty collision with João Pedro.

Jakirovic made bold substitutions. Alonso threw Danny Welbeck on. Palmer scooped over from 20 yards and Tzolakis thwarted Rogers, but Hull had the best chance. Giles crossed again and Mohamed-Ali Cho shot straight at Martínez from close range.

Hull settled for a point. Jakirovic quashed talk of qualifying for Europe, insisting that survival remains the aim. The Bosnian has everyone pulling in the same direction. Before the start of the season he told his staff he would give them seven days off if Hull took eight points from their first five games. Mission completed with a game to spare.

items.title: What can halt Fifa’s authoritarian turn under Infantino? Change from the outside | Jules Boykoff
items.author: Jules Boykoff
items.summary: The 2026 World Cup was a whirling swirl of scintillating soccer that prompted much-needed conversations about the vitality of diaspora, the fortitude of the
items.text:
The 2026 World Cup was a whirling swirl of scintillating soccer that prompted much-needed conversations about the vitality of diaspora, the fortitude of the underdog, the power of sport. In a world fractured along myriad cultural axes floating in an entertainment system dominated by on-demand content, the tournament provided a moment, perhaps unlike any other event, that brought together people from different backgrounds to simultaneously experience something meaningful.

After the tournament concluded, Fifa president Gianni Infantino dropped a political pipebomb into the after-party, proposing to privatize the World Cup by injecting $20bn in private capital, with an assist from JP Morgan and Thrive Capital, the investment vehicle orchestrated by Joshua Kushner, brother to Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

Turns out, Infantino hadn’t just been sucking up to Trump the whole time – from hand-delivering the confected Fifa peace prize to obliging him with the red card reversal heard ’round the world – ostensibly to ensure the World Cup money spigot remained winched wide open. Apparently, Infantino was also studying Trump’s nepotism-flecked smash-and-grab techniques. Not unlike the Trump administration nixing energy-project grants for states “based solely” on whether they supported him in the 2024 presidential election, football associations that backed Infantino’s private-equity scheme would get more money while those that disagreed would receive less. And just as Trump and the rightwing media ecosystem have destabilized the very notion of truth in US political discourse, Fifa subverted the notion of fairness when it nullified the red card for a US player.

But something deeper and even more important is going on. Amid the rising tide of authoritarianism around the world, including in the US under Trump, Fifa under Infantino has itself become increasingly dictatorial. Although Fifa claims it acts “in full respect” of its self-trumpeted “democratic and governance principles”, and that its president’s private-equity fever dream was “about the democratization of football worldwide”, the reality is that Fifa emulates the dictatorships before whom Infantino so readily genuflects. Many within the governing body learned about the privatization gambit through the news rather than proper consultation (just as they had heard of Infantino’s decision to hand Trump the peace prize). Although Fifa statutes limit presidents to “no more than three terms of office”, and Infantino was first elected in 2016 and then re-elected – unopposed by acclamation – in 2019 and 2023, he has declared that he could run again in 2027. Infantino is infamous for besmirching journalists and avoiding press conferences. Tough questions are signs of reporters “spreading hate”. For him, information is meant to flow unidirectionally, cascading from on high.

What can be done? Yes, it’s past time to “give Fifa’s boss the boot”, as a US Soccer vice-president put it. But despite Infantino’s spectacular miscalculations and dictatorial shifts, those who have the power to “boot” him have instead made him the frontrunner in next year’s election. Although soccer’s regional governing bodies in Europe (Uefa), Asia (AFC), as well as North, Central America and the Caribbean (Concacaf) have publicly rebuked Infantino, with Europe even threatening to boycott international competitions, fissures have emerged: Mexico, Qatar and several Asian national associations have broken ranks to signal support for the beleaguered Infantino. The Confederation of African Football (CAF), which represents 54 countries, “unanimously reconfirmed its support” for Infantino, who needs only 106 votes to survive his re-election bid next March. Dislodging Infantino is an uphill fight.

That’s because Fifa’s patronage system is a powerful sedative for dissent: it distributes millions to football associations around the globe under a system of clientelism grounded in fidelity and orchestrated with scant public oversight. This is soccer symbiosis awash in cash and lacking accountability.

Even though Fifa’s proposed privatization could have hurt players, fans and clubs alike, plenty of federations were ready to support it. Sure, private equity has an ignominious record of acquiring holdings with social value, stripping them for parts and leaving a husk of what once was. Exhibit A: sports media. Exhibit B: hospitals. Making football into Exhibit C would not only have risked destroying the world’s most popular sport. It would have been a crime against collective joy. Nevertheless, administrators around the world were happy to back the gambit. This is a testament to the power of that patronage system, built up over decades by successive presidents, from João Havelange to Sepp Blatter to Gianni Infantino.

The top candidates to replace Infantino are freighted with cumbersome baggage. Victor Montagliani rose to become head of Concacaf and a Fifa Council vice-president despite controversial handlings of scandals and partnerships. Another possibility, Fifa Council member Nasser Al-Khelaifi of Qatar, stated that he had “no ambition, no intention and no interest in the Fifa role”. Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, top man at the Asian Football Confederation, already lost to Infantino back in 2016 and has long been dogged by allegations of human-rights violations in Bahrain, which he denies. Lise Klaveness, who heads the Norwegian FA, would bring principle and panache to the presidency – and she has a strong record of standing up to Infantino – but she is essentially unelectable in an organization drenched in sexism.

Let’s be clear: change at Fifa must come from outside the organization. For too long, Fifa has monitored itself. The 2026 World Cup and its aftermath demonstrate unequivocally that Fifa requires independent oversight, toothy regulation carried out by governments and NGOs dedicated to preserving the people’s game as a social good.

Toward that end, FairSquare, the London-based nonprofit human-rights organization on whose advisory board I serve, recently launched a “Reboot Fifa” campaign to declare Infantino ineligible for the March election and to create the biggest-ever class-action complaint against Infantino for openly violating Fifa’s own governing statutes on political neutrality by consistently cozying up to Trump. Donning a red Maga-style cap with “45—47” and “USA” emblazoned on it at a Board of Peace meeting cannot be considered “Fifa remain[ing] neutral in matters of politics”.

Infantino’s clumsy overstepping has galvanized calls for reform and created a chance to reject authoritarianism creep.

Fixing the Fifa greed zombie requires a vibrant pushback on all fronts. We must support Jamie Raskin who, as the ranking member on the House judiciary committee, has demanded Fifa furnish all its documented contact with Trump, members of his administration and the Trump Organization. Switzerland’s parliament should reconsider Fifa’s tax-free status under Swiss law. We should rally behind soccer A-listers like England international Lucy Bronze and former France star Mikaël Silvestre who are insisting that “Change is necessary” and that “enough is enough”. If not now, then when?

items.title: Football lends voice to message worth relaying: men should talk about their pain | Barney Ronay
items.author: Barney Ronay
items.summary: If you watched US television adverts during the World Cup for any length of time one thing just kept leaping out. I’ve mentioned this before here, but it still
items.text:
If you watched US television adverts during the World Cup for any length of time one thing just kept leaping out. I’ve mentioned this before here, but it still seems both jarring and significant. Every third or fourth rotation in that endless daytime scroll, in between the Chicken Megadeth Hyper-Box Family Meal Deal, either side of David Beckham expertly consuming a light beer, is an advert for antidepressants.

The format for these is always the same kind of thing: contented, wholesome people throwing frisbees, or strolling through a small-town antiques fair, while a warm, honeyed, reassuring voiceover talks about how horrifying their lives are, with the suggestion that only a lengthy course of Smileothorium can solve this.

In another world there would be a call to study this phenomenon, to consider why a nation of such dazzling abundance and opportunity should also feel glazed, worthless and deprived of hope. But this is not that world. More than 50 million Americans have depression. This is demand and supply in action, a battle for market share in a £6bn industry. The US often worries about itself in its post-industrial age. What are we now? What can we still make? Where is the new frontier? Well, human misery is looking pretty hot right now.

The reason for talking about this here is that English football is doing a good thing this week. Between 4-14 September the Premier League is sponsoring the Together Against Suicide campaign. Harry Kane and Prince William have spoken warmly in support. The league is posting words of solidarity on its X account, which is probably not the best way to cheer yourself up if we’re being honest.

This is simple, useful messaging. It applies to people of any age, sex or background. But it applies in particular to men, and to middle-aged men, who are more likely to die by suicide than any other age group. Middle-aged men are more likely to experience depression and anxiety in those years. They can be hard to reach because this often happens out of sight or, most heartbreaking of all, without any indication there was even a problem.

It might be a little blunt in its styling. But what football is doing here is unequivocally good. Nothing else has the same level of reach and cut-through. If one person in the line of that message is touched by it, this seems like a happy outcome.

I think I have locus standi to talk about this. Everyone does. It’s universal. But I’m also unarguably a middle-aged man. I have two sons who are also now men. I have middle-aged male friends, many of whom are, with all due respect, a bit loopy. And like so many other people I’ve been down that road some of the way.

Life in Covid really did it for me. Exhaustion, isolation, the inescapable fact of having to carry on existing. Do you really have to, though? This kind of thing can creep into your mind like a shadow, just another idle thought. Until at some point you realise there’s a shadow in the corner of the room, a ghost in the chair, and it’s talking to you.

The fact is, it’s hard to be a man at any age. Or at least, it’s hard in a way that is distinct from other forms of hardness. And yes this statement might fail to draw an overwhelming wave of sympathy, but this is part of the problem. Pain comes for everyone. There’s no hierarchy of suffering. And male pain, male alienation is often carried around like a dead weight for exactly this reason.

Being able to talk about this stuff is the direct opposite of weakness. There is always someone willing to do this with you

double quotation mark

As you get older this can be related to a sense of obsolescence. Men want to do stuff. There’s a kind of programming to feel useful, to serve some kind of function. Frankly, most middle-aged men would be happier if someone just gave them a big piece of wood and told them to saw it in half, then at the end of the day told them they’ve done a really good job, they’re good boys and everyone’s proud of them. Tomorrow you can come back and put it together again.

Instead it can feel like every part of the world is independently conspiring to make you feel like crap. Diminishing work, vanished usefulness, isolation, the way life can exhaust you quietly, without any obvious trauma. Men are not good at processing this. The key method, the strategy we’ve worked out over the years is: don’t process it at all. Carry on. Keep running through the red zone. Lads, it’s not a long-term plan.

I have two pieces of aged wisdom on this front. First, the obvious one. Embrace the feeling and talk about it. Sounds like a cliche. Is actually true. Feeling bad isn’t some deeper, truer version of you. The good stuff also exists and is just as real. Both will pass, and pass again.

Small things do help. Muscular, loud, well‑meaning men on the internet are actually right. Don’t eat rubbish. Get outside. Speak to other people. Remember that the sun also rises, that feeling terrible is also evidence of the ability to feel good. Prince William is right: being able to talk about this stuff is the direct opposite of weakness. There is always someone willing to do this with you, who will like and admire you even more as a result.

The second thing is: you do also have to fight. Those outmoded forms of masculinity – being stoic, resisting your own feelings – tend to get a bad rap. But everyone needs a bit of this. The problem is men are often not taught anything else to go with it.

Life is brutal. It will come for you. It is heroic to fight this, even more so when you’re suffering. Old English poetry is full of epic tales shot through with melancholy warriors weeping at the sadness of the empty hall. In Roman culture the ability to embrace melancholy and fear – as well as scything off the limbs of your enemies – was seen as a sign of great and crowning masculinity. Scipio burnt Carthage to the ground, then sank into a massive depression, at which point he was seen as even more masculine, even more thrillingly in touch with his depths.

Letting it out is strong. Would you like to be a Viking? Or a Roman hero with a sword? Well, those guys spent half their lives in a state of profound inner doubt, telling people all about it, then feeling so much more able to ride off on a horse and do something ostensibly useful.

There is something worth saying about sport in the middle of this. I was at Arsenal last weekend and before kick-off a bubbly and cheerful voice announced: “Suicide is NOT inevitable!” as though what we’re talking about here is having dandruff or not drinking enough water. The messaging is good. The messaging is great. The messaging is also, let’s be honest, an attempt to soothe the effects of the world in which big sport thrives and makes its fortunes. Is this a nice place?

It isn’t hard to work out why American TV is so full of adverts for antidepressants. Take a look at the stuff in between. Terrible, degrading food. Consumer goods you don’t need but must be made to crave. Pills to get you off that addiction to opioids we’ve already given you. Endless excitable messaging from corporations that secretly hate you.

Big Sport does not exist outside of this world. It is part of the same system. Oh, now you care about sad middle-aged men? The same ones who can’t afford to go any more, who feel alienated from what was once a bit of a lark and a chance to get together, whose brains must be subjected to the curated rage of the online idiot-scape?

The note of regret here is that sport still has so much power to be warm, to act as a source of contact. Witness for example the rush of love a few years back when Ben Stokes was able to talk about being depressed while simultaneously operating at his peak as England captain. It felt like a message no one had ever really sent in the same way, that you can feel like this and still be OK, or even heroically functional; that feeling all those things is really just a part of feeling.

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

Scipio burnt Carthage to the ground, then sank into a massive depression, at which point he was seen as even more masculine, even more thrillingly in touch with his depths.
https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3ccb55ac65d1ae03ccd0df84ead9b6bc6d7460f7/0_0_7587_5058/master/7587.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none
blocks.c: Prince William makes a speech at Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium on World Suicide Prevention Day

blocks.x: Letting it out is strong. Would you like to be a Viking? Or a Roman hero with a sword? Well, those guys spent half their lives in a state of profound inner doubt, telling people all about it, then feeling so much more able to ride off on a horse and do something ostensibly useful.

There is something worth saying about sport in the middle of this. I was at Arsenal last weekend and before kick-off a bubbly and cheerful voice announced: “Suicide is NOT inevitable!” as though what we’re talking about here is having dandruff or not drinking enough water. The messaging is good. The messaging is great. The messaging is also, let’s be honest, an attempt to soothe the effects of the world in which big sport thrives and makes its fortunes. Is this a nice place?

It isn’t hard to work out why American TV is so full of adverts for antidepressants. Take a look at the stuff in between. Terrible, degrading food. Consumer goods you don’t need but must be made to crave. Pills to get you off that addiction to opioids we’ve already given you. Endless excitable messaging from corporations that secretly hate you.

Big Sport does not exist outside of this world. It is part of the same system. Oh, now you care about sad middle-aged men? The same ones who can’t afford to go any more, who feel alienated from what was once a bit of a lark and a chance to get together, whose brains must be subjected to the curated rage of the online idiot-scape?

The note of regret here is that sport still has so much power to be warm, to act as a source of contact. Witness for example the rush of love a few years back when Ben Stokes was able to talk about being depressed while simultaneously operating at his peak as England captain. It felt like a message no one had ever really sent in the same way, that you can feel like this and still be OK, or even heroically functional; that feeling all those things is really just a part of feeling.

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

items.text:
Saturday

Golf

6.40am (all times BST)Solheim Cup live

The 20th edition of the Solheim Cup is under way, and for the first time in the Netherlands. Angela Stanford’s Americans are the slight favourites and defending champions, but they have not won on European soil since Germany in 2015. The US, as holders, need only 14 of the 28 points available to retain the crystal trophy. Scott Murray and Matt Cooper offer live coverage of day two’s foursomes (6.40am) and fourballs (12.05am), with Ewan Murray reporting from Bernardus Golf.

Football

8amMatchday live

Join Tom Bassam for the latest news and buildup to Saturday’s football action. We will keep pace with all the day’s breaking news from around the grounds for seven Premier League matches, plus a full Championship and EFL programme. Join our Matchday live community by sending your thoughts and queries to matchday.live@theguardian.com.

Premier League

3pmClockwatch

Barry Glendenning keeps watch over all five 3pm kick-offs in the Premier League, and will be focusing on two of the afternoon’s most compelling games. Liverpool’s season took ⁠a while to get going under Andoni Iraola but after wins at Ipswich and then Atlético Madrid in the Champions League they will relish another home clash against a Fulham side managed by the former Liverpool player Álvaro Arbeloa. After three successive defeats and seven goals conceded, Arbeloa is already feeling the pressure of management in the top flight. Alongside last season’s top two, only promoted Hull remain unbeaten but their brilliant start faces an acid test against Xabi Alonso’s free-scoring Chelsea.

Formula One

3pmSpanish Grand Prix qualifying live

Kimi Antonelli is Formula One’s man of the moment but Mercedes’ 20-year-old championship leader faces a Monumental challenge in Spain this weekend, along with all his rivals. Fresh from ⁠becoming the first Italian since ⁠1966 to win his home race at Monza, Antonelli will be entering new territory when the Spanish capital’s Madring makes its grand prix debut with its signature La Monumental. The banked curve is a 550m-long high-speed 270-degree bend with a crest on the exit meaning drivers momentarily take it blind as they look up at the sky. Mercedes, winners of nine ‌of the first 13 races, should be in the mix but can expect a tougher fight than Monza, where they finished one-two, putting Antonelli 66 points clear of ‌his teammate George Russell. We will have lap-by-lap coverage of qualifying from Philip Cornwall, and Giles Richards reporting from Madrid.

Premier League

5.30pmTottenham v Everton live

Despite a £300m close-season splurge, Roberto De Zerbi’s Spurs are winless in their first three games and without a goal. Little more than three months ago, the Italian completed his Tottenham rescue mission as they beat Everton on the final day of the season to secure their top-flight status. On Saturday, David Moyes’ Everton are the visitors again and, while the stakes are not so high, De Zerbi desperately needs a victory to instil some belief that the money has been well spent. There will be a live blog of the match, with David Hytner reporting from Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Tennis

7pmUS Open women’s singles final

Elena Rybakina rallied to beat Coco Gauff in a thrilling semi-final to earn a title showdown with the defending champion, Aryna Sabalenka, and take a step towards her third grand slam crown. The pair have met in two previous slam finals, with Sabalenka defeating Rybakina in the 2023 Australian Open decider before the second seed ​levelled the score at Melbourne Park in ‌January. Sabalenka, who will lose her world No 1 status to her opponent on Monday regardless of the result, is seeking to join Chris Evert and Serena Williams as the only women to win three straight US Open titles. Katy Murrells helms the live blog, with Tumaini Carayol reporting from Flushing Meadows.

Premier League

8pmSunderland v Arsenal live

Stability has been the order of the day at Arsenal, with Mikel Arteta’s side straight back into last term’s groove. Arsenal visit Sunderland, a fixture they will be wary of after being held to a 2-2 draw at the Stadium of Light last season. The Gunners made it four wins from four with a 1-0 victory at Napoli in their Champions League opener on Wednesday night and – with three victories in the Premier League already under their belt – show no signs of faltering. Billy Munday liveblogs the match and Louise Taylor reports.

Rugby union

10pmSouth Africa v New Zealand live

After three bruising contests, South Africa go in search of a third successive Test victory over ⁠the All Blacks that would secure the four-game series for the world champions and lay down a marker for next year’s title defence. The ⁠final game of New ⁠Zealand’s six-week, ​eight-match tour of South Africa is being played in the United States as the top-ranked sides in the world look ⁠to promote the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series to a wider audience at the 70,000-seater home of the NFL’s Baltimore Ravens. Daniel Gallan buckles up as blog host.

Sunday

Boxing

3amRyan Garcia v Conor Benn live

Ryan Garcia enters his WBC welterweight title fight showdown with Conor Benn carrying the belt but understanding that winning the belt and establishing himself as a legitimate champion are different accomplishments. The American captured the first recognised world title of his turbulent career in February, dominating his compatriot Mario Barrios over 12 rounds for a unanimous decision. The performance showcased a more disciplined, complete fighter than the social media phenomenon who built his reputation on blinding speed and a devastating left hook. Now he must prove that victory began a sustained championship run. His first defence comes at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas, where personal hostility and contrasting styles should produce a revealing test. The British fighter intends to pressure Garcia, force exchanges and make the fight physical. Bryan Armen Graham has round-by-round coverage of the big fight.

Football

8amMatchday live

Emillia Hawkins clocks on bright and early to preview Sunday’s action with breaking news and much more as we settle down for two Premier League fixtures, with all the noise around the afternoon’s Manchester derby. Email matchday.live@theguardian.com with your notions and queries.

Golf

10.10amSolheim Cup live

Scott Murray is back at post for the deciding singles contests as Europe seek to regain the trophy after losing 15½-12½ in Virginia two years ago in the biggest team event in women’s golf.

Women’s Super League

12pmManchester United v Chelsea live

Emillia Hawkins then turns to live commentary as last season’s fourth- and third-place teams respectively meet for the first time this season, both seeking a first win of the campaign. United lost to London City last weekend as Eva Olid took charge of the club for the first time in the WSL while Sonia Bompastor’s Chelsea were held by Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge despite battering the visitors with 35 shots. Suzanne Wrack reports.

Scottish League Cup quarter-final

12pmRangers v Celtic live

The Hoops’ only blemish this term remains their Champions League playoff capitulation away to Lask, and overcoming their Old Firm rivals at Ibrox to reach the semi-final of the Premier Sports Cup would help maintain their momentum. There will, however, be no Celtic fans in attendance after the recent decision not to allow away supporters at any matches between the two Glasgow giants this term to avoid the trouble that marred last season’s Scottish Cup collision. The anxiety from the Light Blues legions, which has been prevalent in some games in Govan, resurfaced on Wednesday night as the home side struggled in the Premiership match against St Mirren after missing several chances before the break. However, a pressure valve was released when Bojan Miovski scored in stoppage time for a crucial 1-0 win, making it four victories in a row for Derek McInnes and his side. Taha Hashim liveblogs the cup tie, and Paul MacInnes reports.

Formula One

2pmSpanish Grand Prix

John Brewin has lap-by-lap coverage as Formula One sweeps into Madrid for a first look at the Madring. Mercedes are in the ascendant and Kimi Antonelli can still put the equivalent of three race wins between him and Russell, with the Briton chasing a first win since Austria in June to prevent his title hopes from withering further. McLaren, who won in the Netherlands and Hungary with the reigning world champion, Lando Norris, and have Oscar Piastri hungry to open his account, could be the main rivals. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc drove the Madring when it was still a building site on a scorching filming day in July but there is an underlying tension in the camp after last weekend’s opening-lap shenanigans at Monza.

Premier League

4.30pmManchester United v Manchester City live

After all the pre-season optimism, United’s start to the season has been inconsistent but Sunday’s derby offers Michael Carrick’s side an early chance ⁠to show they are contenders. City, meanwhile, arrive at Old Trafford with a perfect record under their new manager, Enzo Maresca, although their performances have suggested there is still work to do after Pep Guardiola’s departure. Carrick’s impact at United last season as interim manager after the club’s parting of ways with Ruben Amorim in January was dramatic, beginning with a 2-0 home victory over City. Their rivals will provide an acid test, especially with Erling Haaland firing on all cylinders having scored both goals in the 2-0 win at Porto in the Champions League on Tuesday to make it five goals in three games so far this season. Rob Smyth liveblogs the big game of the weekend, with Jamie Jackson and Will Unwin reporting from Old Trafford.

Tennis

7pmUS Open men’s singles final

The men’s singles semis pitted Alexander Zverev against Karen Khachanov and Frances Tiafoe with Ben Shelton. The latter pairing are on a quest to become the first American men’s grand slam champion ⁠since Andy Roddick’s 2003 triumph at Flushing Meadows. Whoever emerges victorious will collide in Sunday evening’s final, and Ella Brockway has live blog commentary of the showdown.

items.title: 高盛TMT大会第三天：黄仁勋回击“循环融资”质疑——“投1块拿回100块？那就多来点”
items.summary: 人工智能基础设施投资浪潮正在提速，而非降温。在高盛年度科技盛会Communacopia + Technology
items.text:
人工智能基础设施投资浪潮正在提速，而非降温。在高盛年度科技盛会Communacopia + Technology Conference第三天，来自英伟达、SpaceX、CrowdStrike等科技巨头的高管传递出一致信号：算力、电力与数据中心容量——而非终端需求——才是当前制约AI增长的核心瓶颈，而这一瓶颈预计将持续至2028年。


英伟达CEO黄仁勋重申2030年AI基础设施市场规模将达3万亿至4万亿美元，并明确表示公司2027财年70%的营收增长目标受限于供应而非需求。SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen则披露公司正朝着年化1000亿美元总营收目标迈进，并计划于2027年部署AI卫星，将轨道算力成本压至与地面算力相当的水平。高盛银行家将AI定性为"投资超级周期"而非泡沫，但同时指出，超大规模云厂商能否将资本支出积压转化为持久企业收入，仍是市场最核心的悬念。


网络安全成为本届大会最高频的议题之一。黄仁勋明确将网络安全列为AI的下一个主要应用场景，Palo Alto Networks CEO直言"AI安全行业甚至尚未建立"，而CrowdStrike与Palo Alto两家公司合计市值约4900亿美元，与万亿级AI公司相比仍存在显著估值差距，引发市场对该赛道重估空间的关注。


黄仁勋：70%增长是供应上限，不是需求上限


黄仁勋在接受高盛半导体分析师James Schneider访谈时，系统阐述了AI基础设施高速增长的底层逻辑。他将驱动力归结为两个叠加的行业变革：从检索式计算向生成式计算的范式转移，以及摩尔定律的终结。


在他看来，过去60年的计算机本质上是"预先录制"的——用户点击后从存储中检索信息。但生成式AI要求实时基于上下文生成答案，这意味着一个全新的、持续运转的计算层必须被建造。与此同时，晶体管缩小红利消失，性能提升不再依赖制程微缩，英伟达的应对是通过CoWoS多芯片封装与NVLink纵向扩展实现极端协同设计。黄仁勋强调：

"如果你没有NVLink，如果你不能有真正出色的纵向扩展，你就死定了，因为摩尔定律是你的敌人。"

黄仁勋重申，英伟达2027财年70%的同比营收增长目标是供应上限而非需求上限——若无供应约束，增速将更高。分析师预计英伟达本财年营收约4000亿美元，按70%增幅计算，明年营收将达约6800亿美元。他同时将英伟达在AI供应链中的地位与台积电相提并论，强调每一家AI实验室都能在英伟达平台上构建业务，"某种程度上就像台积电"。


在供应约束方面，黄仁勋承认上游封装、晶圆、内存以及下游数据中心电力与选址均存在广泛瓶颈，但强调英伟达的生态系统规模与客户可见度是应对这些约束的核心优势，并维持CY27约70%同比增长的预期。


正面回击"循环融资"质疑


黄仁勋在大会上直接回应了市场对英伟达5000亿美元融资平台的"循环融资"质疑。争议源于英伟达今年8月宣布与Apollo、BlackRock、Blackstone、Brookfield、高盛及KKR等金融机构合作成立算力融资平台，计划募集超过5000亿美元第三方资金，支持AI模型开发商兴建基础设施。


批评者担忧，英伟达投资AI公司或云服务商，这些公司再回购英伟达硬件，投资与销售之间的界线趋于模糊——这一模式在上一轮互联网基础设施热潮中曾导致朗讯科技等供应商走向衰落。


黄仁勋以财务数据正面反驳："我看了一下财务报表，我们投入1美元、拿回100美元的回报，这算是循环融资吗？如果这也算，那我们就多做一些。"他强调，在动用公司资金投资之前，英伟达会确认被投资方手中有真实合同、能从客户处获得收入，他见过的此类合同总额达1000亿美元。


高盛的研究报告亦指出，英伟达的财务担保旨在为生态系统提供种子资金，但最终回报规模及投资方的多元化，与"循环融资"的定义并不相符。


SpaceX：从火箭运营商到AI基础设施平台


SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen的演讲是本届大会另一大亮点。他明确表示，SpaceX正将自身定位为一体化AI基础设施平台，而非单纯的发射或卫星运营商，垂直整合覆盖火箭、电力、算力基础设施、AI模型、客户关系与Starlink连接。


关键数据披露包括：公司目前算力收益处于每吉瓦300亿至500亿美元区间的上限；本月初完成一笔新的算力授权协议；对年底前实现年化1000亿美元总营收的信心进一步增强；预计2026年底算力规模扩展至超过2GW，2027年底达5至10GW。


在轨道算力方面，SpaceX计划于2027年部署AI卫星，并预计轨道算力成本达到与地面算力相当水平的时间将早于此前预期。Starlink宽带业务持续增长，企业与政府服务表现尤为突出，Starlink Mobile预计于2028年上半年推出。Johnsen将AI模型、地面算力、Starlink、星舰与轨道算力整合为一个统一的基础设施增长叙事。


网络安全：AI时代最被低估的赛道


网络安全是本届大会出现频率最高的议题，黄仁勋、Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora与CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz均从不同角度强调了这一赛道的战略价值。


黄仁勋的逻辑链清晰：AI加速自动化编程，代码生成速度提升意味着代码被利用和攻击的速度同步加快，漏洞修复需求随之激增。


“还有什么比制造一个问题更能创造需求呢？”他表示，网络安全需要持续运作，将为AI大型实验室带来庞大新商机。目前英伟达正与CrowdStrike、思科、Palantir合作，使用Nemotron模型构建红蓝队系统。


Arora则指出，AI正在加速漏洞发现与攻击复杂度，企业需要集成化安全平台而非碎片化供应商堆叠。Palo Alto拥有约1.8亿个已部署传感器，每日处理19PB数据，构成数据与训练护城河。他直言“AI安全行业甚至尚未建立”，而未来五年5万亿美元的算力投资将带来网络流量的大幅增长，全部需要安全检测。


CrowdStrike的Kurtz则强调，公司10年以上的专有标注安全数据是核心竞争壁垒，其域专用模型的修复成本约为每次活动0.03美元，而前沿模型替代方案约为10美元，但可实现相近效果。新产品Guardian早期需求强劲，Flex协议累计达935笔，灵活性承诺总额23亿美元，上季度Flex交易量环比增长两倍。


SpaceX之外：Uber、MongoDB与Mastercard的AI叙事


Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi重申增长由出行与外卖双轮驱动。Uber One会员数量突破5000万，同比增长50%，占总订单量约50%，会员消费额是非会员的2至3倍。外卖业务中，杂货与零售年化营收达150亿美元，同比增长超40%，管理层认为按需零售规模最终可能超过出行业务。Uber同时表示，目标是在2028至2029年成为领先的自动驾驶商业化平台。


MongoDB CEO CJ Desai等管理层强调公司正演变为双引擎增长模式，Atlas连续五个季度维持约29%增长，Enterprise Advanced ARR连续三个季度增长超10%。AI方面，Voyage正通过Claude Code、Codex等编程代理成为客户获取渠道，客户数量环比近乎翻倍；Managed MCP发布有助于将Atlas直接嵌入代理驱动的开发工作流。AI辅助现代化迁移有望将项目周期从18至24周压缩至4至8周。


Mastercard CFO Ling Hai指出，消费者与企业支出趋势在8月保持强劲，跨境交易健康，无卡支付增长越来越多由AI订阅、数字资产等数字原生支付流驱动。服务业务目前占净营收近40%，网络安全需求在收购Recorded Future后持续加速，中国市场在获得国内牌照后仍是中期重要机遇。


半导体设备：供需持续偏紧，能见度"史无前例"


Lam Research CFO Doug Bettinger在大会上措辞强硬，称行业"基本上已售罄"，管理层更担心错过上行空间而非应对下行周期。Lam预计2027年晶圆设备支出（WFE）增长由DRAM主导，先进逻辑/代工紧随其后，NAND亦将稳健增长，洁净室可用性是关键约束，预计至2027年底前持续存在。


值得关注的新信息包括：Lam已与SpaceX的Terafab项目深度合作，该项目被描述为"非常大的机遇"；公司宣布在美国投资30亿美元用于实验室与工程建设，包括新建俄勒冈实验室；中国WFE今年小幅增长，但占比持续下降。


Seagate CFO Gianluca Romano则表示，AI基础设施驱动的存储需求叠加有限的供给增长，将持续支撑定价上行，上季度每艾字节价格同比上涨约11%。HAMR技术出货量有望于2026年底在艾字节维度超越PMR，预计未来几年占公司出货量的80%至90%。


高盛结论：超级周期而非泡沫，但ROI仍是核心考验


高盛科技研究主管James Schneider与欧洲TMT专家Sean Johnstone均在总结中强调，AI需求正在跨越整个技术栈持续扩展，但市场辩论已从模型能力转向基础设施规模、电力、投资回报率与真实企业落地。


高盛银行家将AI定性为投资超级周期而非泡沫，底部指标仍具建设性——供给偏紧、算力需求强劲、产品创新提速。但宏观层面的顾虑依然存在：利率、地缘政治、政策不确定性以及大数定律。


Johnstone的核心判断一语中的：AI需求正在扩展，但投资者仍需要证明资本支出能够转化为持久收入、利润率与现金流。

超大规模云厂商需要将积压订单转化为持续的企业AI收入，客户正从“最大化算力消耗”转向“以ROI为导向的算力优化”，而电力、内存、数据中心建设与容量方面的约束，可能使市场持续偏紧至2028年。

超大规模云厂商需要将积压订单转化为持续的企业AI收入，客户正从“最大化算力消耗”转向“以ROI为导向的算力优化”，而电力、内存、数据中心建设与容量方面的约束，可能使市场持续偏紧至2028年。
